name: Gareth Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 58, lead developer at a tech company that builds public-water alerts. I have a master's degree and know our lab-data exceptions well, though I still ask technicians to sign a repeat sample before I release a warning. I have never used AI tools. My partner is a school secretary, our daughter has grown, and we are paying a manageable mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the water lab that a contamination warning has to match the sample bottle and the lab's signed result. I lead software for a tech company's public-water alert system and have never used AI tools; I check a disputed warning against the bench log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, our work and money should be all right. I have a master's degree and a typical senior wage, my partner is a full-time school secretary, and we have four months of expenses saved while paying a manageable mortgage; there are some software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking alert-release bugs against signed sample results and the lab's bench log. We'd put another 80 monthly into savings while both wages hold, because the mortgage and retirement figures still need paying and checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about present income. A false all-clear on drinking water still has to be caught before a neighbourhood turns on its taps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you hold the all-clear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The screen showed the reservoir sample as clear, but the lab had marked the bottle for a repeat test. I held the public water all-clear until the second signed lab result arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter works in another town. We enjoy her visits, but her wages are for her own life, not our mortgage.

I'd hold **public all-clears** until repeat samples are checked.
think: I expect **both wages** and my lead job to hold under mild change.
I have **four months saved** and a manageable mortgage.
do: Keep **checking alert releases** against signed lab samples and bench logs.
Save **80 extra monthly** while both wages hold and mortgage payments continue.
feel: **Calm** about current income, vigilant about false water clears.

fieldNote: **Two steady wages** and four months saved support calm despite a manageable mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may write warning code and answer residents, but lab staff need a paid way to stop a false all-clear. I want any new system checked with the people who handle the bottles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead experience may matter, yet the company could still cut reviewers after software takes ordinary tests. Four months saved helps, but my partner's school wage alone would not cover our mortgage and all bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the lab staff group and our union branch in one signed request for missed-warning counts and a named paid release stopper. I'd keep bringing signed repeat-sample cases to the weekly review and postpone a planned garden paving job until the firm writes down our paid staffing hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the post. A tidy dashboard could hide a missed sample. We can pay this month, but I cannot assume the lead title protects my next year’s wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When should a repeat sample clear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A repeat sample should stay pending until the lab signs the second result. If the app turns it green because the first number was low, the warning fails the exact situation we need it for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union and lab group would sign together and request a dated answer. A single email from me would not give the technicians a lasting voice in the release.

I'd keep **paid stop authority** on public all-clears.
think: I could lose **lead review hours** despite my experience.
I cannot cover **mortgage and bills** on school-secretary pay alone.
do: Join **lab and union group** requesting missed-warning counts and paid release-stop duties.
Keep **repeat-sample cases** in weekly alert review.

feel: **Anxious** about pay and an unsafe public all-clear.

fieldNote: **Warning code** and resident replies face AI, putting his own paid lead hours at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write water-alert code before sampling robots arrive around 2031. A resident should still be able to ask who signed a public all-clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my lead review post quickly. My partner's school wage pays some bills, but not the mortgage and all health costs; four months saved would buy a search, not an early retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the water utility and three nearby tech firms about actual paid lab-record, alert-review or software vacancies and written pay. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose wages with my partner's cover mortgage, food, health and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work while using the reserve and call the lender before an overdue payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the larger wage, even with four months to look. I cannot turn a signed lab result into a signed job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the anonymised reservoir repeat-sample correction and the held all-clear. A hiring manager can see why the first low number was not enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner needs the new job's hours and health cover in writing. If school hours are lost, the remaining combined wage must still cover the mortgage and health costs.

I'd check **real paid vacancies** before promising a fallback.
think: I expect **my lead review post** could go quickly.
I cannot cover **mortgage and health** on school wages alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us build enough cash to avoid making a job decision with the mortgage due tomorrow. Thinking AI reaches my code then; sampling robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still lose lead hours before 2031, so I will not count five more years of pay. We have four months saved today, and I want six, but the extra money must come from actual wages, not my daughter's account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the repeat-sample review and ask the lab and union group to request a written paid stop-duty agreement before the new software is installed. Starting now we'd save 180 monthly while both wages hold, stopping that extra transfer if either wage falls; in the first year after 2031 I'd keep the paid release role only while hours and stop authority are written down, otherwise seek a signed nearby job whose combined wages cover mortgage, food, health and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the post, but a six-month reserve would let us read a real offer rather than accept a rumour. I still need a paid job, even if the lab trusts my judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the stop-duty agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stop-duty agreement should name who can hold an all-clear while a repeat bottle is tested, and how many paid hours that review gets. An unpaid signature is not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a wage drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will look at our account each month. If school or developer pay drops, we protect the current four months before trying to reach six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 may take me to 68, but thinking AI would still reach water-alert code before sampling robots around 2039. I want the lab's repeat test legible long after my name leaves the release sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today both wages and four months saved keep the mortgage manageable. I have not verified our pension figures, and I cannot assume the firm will pay me for ten more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the repeat-test record and save 80 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare verified amounts with mortgage, food, health and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover the bills; otherwise I'd keep an available paid role or seek real local openings without counting our daughter's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant work, but our present bills are covered. I will not replace a signed monthly amount with a hopeful retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The record should show the first sample, the repeat request and the signed second result. A new developer must see why we held the public all-clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter support retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter can share a meal with us whenever she visits. Her wages belong to her own household, and I would not write them into our plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could cut lead review before a water utility or nearby company offers paid work. Written cut timing, real vacancies and a lender discussion before arrears would help us protect the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who may stop a public all-clear while the lab repeats a bottle. A named person needs paid hours and real authority to hold that release; an empty signature box protects nobody.

headlineQuote: A named person needs paid hours and real authority to hold that release; an empty signature box protects nobody.

He will **verify retirement income** against mortgage and health costs rather than assume his grown daughter's pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his lead wage before another paid review post appears.
